catalog_quote: [Blevins 2025: 142] As for whether there are languages (outside Austronesian) with tonic gemination after all vowels, the answer appears to be yes. One of these is Kugu Nganhcara, a Pama-Nyungan language of Australia, as described by Smith & Johnson (2000). In this language, with consonants /p, t, t̪, c, k, b, d, d̪, j, g, m, n, n̪, ɲ, ŋ, l, r, w, j/, all consonants except the tap, /r/, have geminate allophones optionally in intervocalic position following a short initial stressed syllable. || [Verstraete 2021 MS: 17] There are three indications that the original stress system in Umpithamu must have been one that was left-aligned, with a leftmost stress rule. The first indication is local, relating to Umpithamu's closest relatives. Most other Middle Paman languages for which we have a reliable description of word stress have a system of this kind: this is the case, for instance, in Wik Mungkan (Kilham 1974), Kugu Nganhcara (Smith & Johnson 2000), Wik Ngathan (Sutton 1978) and possibly also Umpila (Thompson 1988). || [Smith & Johnson 1986: 30-31] There are six patrilects: Kugu Muminh, Kugu Uwanh, Kugu Ugbanh, Kugu Mu'inh, Kugu Yi'anh and Wik Iyanh ... Wik Iyanh speakers are inland rather than coastal people and are somewhat peripheral to the Nganhcara group. On linguistic grounds, however, Wik Iyanh is clearly a Kugu Nganhcara patrilect (see section 3).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand and indirect: for the Kugu Nganhcara patrilect cluster (which Smith & Johnson 2000 take to include Wik Iyanh), word stress is on the initial syllable (the 'tonic' syllable after which consonants geminate). No first-hand statement specific to Wik-Iiyanh was accessible; corroborating generic second-hand remarks: Blevins 2001:487 ('the Wik languages.. word-initial stressed syllables and post-tonic gemination', Alpher pers. comm.) and Sutton 1978 / Sutton & Hale 2021 fn.5 (first-vowel primary stress, but stated for Wik-Ngathan/Wik-Ngatharr).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing reported second-hand for Kugu Nganhcara/Wik Iyanh.
new_statements.exceptions: None in the second-hand report (gemination is limited to position after a SHORT initial stressed syllable, which concerns gemination, not stress placement).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level implied ('initial stressed syllable' of the word); the primary source's own formulation, domain and any compound/enclitic provisions (Kugu Nganhcara has atonic enclitic pronouns per Hale in Sutton & Hale 2021:199-201) remain unseen.
new_statements.identity_note: The only accessible stress information is for 'Kugu Nganhcara' (WALS knc; Glottolog splits the cluster into Wik-Ngenchera wikn1246, Kuku-Muminh kuku1283, Kuku-Uwanh, Kuku-Mu'inh, Kuku-Ugbanh kuku1281, Kuku-Mangk and Wik-Iiyanh wiki1239). Smith & Johnson 2000 treat Wik Iyanh as one of the Kugu Nganhcara patrilects (confirmed by Sutton & Hale 2021:83, 98 citing S&J 2000:364, and by a Handbook snippet 'WIK IYANH FORMS.. differences from the system presented above'), while Glottolog files Wik-Iiyanh under Mungkan-Mungkanhu with Wik-Mungkan (wikm1247); Sutton & Hale 2021 note the equation Wik-Iiyanh = Wik-Iiyeny = Wik-Iiyanyi = Mungkanhu is doubtful and that these names 'probably refer to a number of distinct dialects' (Sutton 1978). Any catalog entry built from the Kugu Nganhcara description should flag that it is a cluster-level statement, not Wik-Iiyanh-specific.

sources.citation: Sutton, Peter & Ken Hale. 2021. Linguistic Organisation and Native Title: The Wik Case, Australia. Canberra: ANU Press (Asia-Pacific Linguistics), open-access PDF.
sources.note: No Wik-Iiyanh stress statement. Wik-Iyanh treated as a named variety that 'in terms of phonological developments, morphology and morphophonology.. belongs more with the Kugu Ngancharra subgroup' (p.98, citing Smith & Johnson 2000:364; also p.83). Stress mentioned only in Hale's ch.7 for Wik-Me'nh/Wik-Mungkan (free pronouns 'carry stress or accent', enclitics atonic, reduction of unstressed CV vowels, p.181) and Sutton's fn.5 p.182 (first-syllable vowel = 'the vowel with primary word stress', explicitly for Wik-Ngathan/Wik-Ngatharr orthography).
